item.title: Housing market steadies but rent rise expectations surge
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market is showing tentative signs of stabilisation, with buyer demand and agreed sales improving in August, according to the latest RICS UK Residential Market Survey. However, the market remains fragile, with ongoing uncertainty around interest rates and broader economic factors continuing to weigh on confidence.

Modest improvements in buyer activity

August saw a fifth consecutive monthly improvement in new buyer enquiries, with the net balance rising to -19%, the least negative reading since January. Agreed sales also strengthened, with the net balance improving to -17%, up from -38% in April. This marks the strongest performance since February, suggesting a gradual recovery in activity.

Looking ahead, expectations for sales over the next three months edged closer to neutral, with the net balance improving to -3% in August. Over the next 12 months, a net balance of +6% of survey respondents anticipate an increase in sales volumes, up from +3% previously. Jeremy Leaf, North London estate agent and former RICS residential chairman, noted that a modest uptick in demand has coincided with holidaymakers returning to the market, though activity remains lower than this time last year.

House prices remain under pressure

While buyer activity has improved slightly, house prices continue to face downward pressure. The headline price balance edged up to -28% in August, from -29% in July, but remains firmly in negative territory. Survey respondents expect prices to fall in the short term, with the 12-month outlook remaining broadly flat.

Regional variations persist, with London recording a more negative price balance than the national average, despite slight improvements from July. In contrast, Northern Ireland continues to buck the trend, with respondents reporting rising prices. The North West of England also showed relative resilience compared to other regions.

Rising rental expectations

Whilst the sales market remains subdued, expectations for rental price increases have surged. Survey respondents anticipate significant upward pressure on rents in the coming months, driven by a combination of strong tenant demand and a lack of available rental properties. This trend could place further strain on renters, particularly in urban areas where demand is highest.

The outlook for the housing market remains uncertain, with factors such as mortgage rates, inflation, and potential tax changes in the Budget likely to influence activity in the coming months. Borrowers and homeowners may wish to stay informed about market developments and seek professional advice to navigate this complex landscape.

As the autumn property market season approaches, sustained activity will depend on whether economic conditions remain stable. For now, the market appears to be moving sideways, with cautious optimism tempered by ongoing challenges.

item.title: Regional deadlines unveiled for new national landlord register
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The government has announced regional rollout dates for England’s new Private Rented Sector Database, revealing when landlords must register their rental properties between 2026 and 2027. The phased introduction begins in the West Midlands, with other regions following monthly until completion in November 2027.

Registration deadlines by region

Landlords with assured or regulated tenancies must register each rental property they own, providing personal details, tenancy information and safety certification. The registration fee stands at £65 per property, renewable annually. Here are the regional deadlines:

  • West Midlands: 14 March 2027
  • East of England: 14 April 2027
  • East Midlands: 14 May 2027
  • South East: 14 June 2027
  • Yorkshire and the Humber: 14 July 2027
  • North West: 14 August 2027
  • North East: 14 September 2027
  • London: 14 October 2027
  • South West: 14 November 2027

Property owners who miss their regional deadline could face financial penalties. The database will require up-to-date gas safety certificates, electrical installation condition reports and Energy Performance Certificate ratings.

Implications for letting agents

While landlords must complete the registration process themselves, letting agents will play a supporting role in the new system. Agents will eventually need to include registration numbers in property listings and may assist landlords with uploading required documentation.

Industry body Propertymark has raised concerns about the registration being landlord-only. Timothy Douglas, their Head of Policy and Campaigns, noted: "Letting agents frequently manage properties on landlords’ behalf, yet can’t register properties directly. This could create administrative bottlenecks as each landlord must register separately."

Agents will however be permitted to upload safety certificates and property details if authorised by the landlord. The phased rollout aims to give all parties time to prepare, though some industry voices suggest a centralised agent registration system might improve efficiency.

Landlords and agents may wish to note their regional deadline well in advance, as the database becomes a mandatory requirement for all private rented properties in England. The government intends the system to improve standards and transparency in the private rental sector.

item.title: Agents warned of major workload from new landlord database
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The government's new Private Rented Sector Database is set to launch regionally as part of the Renters’ Rights Act, requiring landlords to register properties at £65 per year. While industry bodies welcome clarity on timelines, concerns persist about duplicative costs, enforcement effectiveness, and potential gaps in improving rental standards.

Mixed industry response to landlord database

The National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) acknowledges the benefits of a clear implementation timetable but warns the database risks becoming a superficial landlord directory rather than a robust compliance tool. NRLA chief executive Ben Beadle suggests the system should actively verify property standards and ownership using existing data, rather than relying on landlords to self-report documents.

Industry professionals highlight that many landlords already pay for local licensing schemes collecting similar information. The NRLA urges the government to clarify how these parallel systems will integrate to avoid duplicate costs and administrative burdens. Without proper coordination, compliant landlords might effectively pay twice for providing identical information through different schemes.

Potential enforcement complications

Legal experts caution that overlapping registration regimes could create confusion around enforcement. Property disputes specialists note landlords might theoretically face penalties under both national and local schemes for the same issues. This raises questions about how enforcement priorities will be determined between different authorities.

The current proposal leaves several practical questions unanswered:

  • How local licensing data will integrate with the national system
  • Whether registration fees will replace or supplement existing local charges
  • How councils will utilise the database for targeted enforcement
  • What verification processes will ensure data accuracy

Housing campaigners argue the database should actively drive up standards by making non-compliance harder to conceal, rather than simply creating an address list of rental properties. Some suggest linking registration to mandatory property inspections or existing energy performance certificates to verify living conditions.

Looking ahead

As the rollout progresses, landlords and letting agents may wish to monitor how regional implementations address these concerns. The database's ultimate success may depend on whether it evolves into an intelligent compliance tool or remains a basic registration portal. With the private rented sector playing an increasingly vital role in the UK housing market, getting this balance right could benefit tenants, landlords and local authorities alike.

item.title: Buyer demand jumps as September housing market springs to life
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK housing market has shown signs of renewed vigour as buyer demand surged at the start of September, according to the latest data from Rightmove. The property portal reported a 5% increase in buyer activity during the first week of the month, significantly higher than the average 0.4% rise typically seen over the past five years. This uptick suggests that potential homebuyers returned to the market more swiftly after the summer break, though demand remains 9% lower than the same period last year.

Regional Variations in Buyer Demand

Rightmove’s data highlights that every region across Great Britain experienced an increase in buyer demand during early September. London led the way with a notable 9% rise, followed closely by the South West at 8%. The West Midlands and North East both recorded increases of around 7%, while the East Midlands and South East saw a 6% uplift. Other regions, including the East of England and North West, also saw modest gains. Wales and Scotland, however, experienced more subdued growth, with increases of 3% and 1% respectively.

Factors Influencing the Market

The stronger-than-usual September bounce follows a challenging summer for the housing market, which faced headwinds from economic uncertainty, geopolitical tensions, and extreme weather conditions. Whilst the latest figures indicate a promising start to the autumn selling season, it’s worth noting that buyer demand remains below last year’s levels. Property commentators suggest that whilst the increase is encouraging, it may take further weeks to assess whether this trend will sustain and narrow the annual gap.

Colleen Babcock, Rightmove’s property commentator, commented: “It’s positive to see buyers re-engaging with the market as we move into autumn. However, with the month still in its early stages, it’s important to monitor how this momentum develops in the coming weeks.”

For homeowners considering selling, this uptick in demand could present an opportune moment to list their property. Borrowers might also wish to explore mortgage options to capitalise on the renewed activity in the market. As the autumn season progresses, it remains to be seen whether this early September boost will translate into sustained growth across the UK housing market.

item.title: Zoopla wins back major estate agency but agent numbers remain undisclosed
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The South West's property market has seen a significant boost with regional heavyweight Stags Estate Agents rejoining Zoopla's platform. The independent agency, which operates across more than 25 locations in Devon, Cornwall, Somerset and Dorset, has signed a three-year partnership deal with the property portal. This agreement marks Stags' return to Zoopla after previously using the platform.

What the new partnership means

Under the agreement, Stags will list properties on Zoopla while also utilising the portal's valuation lead services to generate new business opportunities. The estate agency specialises in valuation-led services, making Zoopla's lead generation capabilities particularly valuable for their operations.

Lee Flay, partner at Stags, commented: "Zoopla's strength in delivering high-quality valuation leads was pivotal in our decision. Their ongoing platform investments align perfectly with our marketing needs, while their strong London presence offers valuable exposure to potential South West buyers."

Zoopla's growing influence

While Zoopla hasn't disclosed current agency numbers, the portal revealed its homeowner subscriber base has doubled in two years, now exceeding six million. Their latest marketing push highlights the commercial potential of this audience – claiming South West homeowners using their platform generated over £200m in potential agent commissions.

The portal also noted that 17% of homebuyers looking at South West properties originate from other UK regions. This matches Stags' existing strategy of targeting London and Home Counties buyers through its partnership with The London Office.

Paul Whitehead, Zoopla's CEO, stated: "Stags' decision to partner with us for three years strongly endorses our valuation capabilities and lead quality. We're focused on delivering them a robust return on investment."

The Stags agreement forms part of Zoopla's wider expansion strategy, following their recent return to profitability. The portal has been actively securing new partnerships while enhancing its platform services for both homeowners and agents.

For prospective homebuyers in the South West, this partnership could mean access to more comprehensive property listings, while homeowners might benefit from increased exposure for their properties through Stags' expanded marketing reach.

item.title: Rental growth accelerating in half of England’s regions
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Rental Price Surges Reported Across Multiple English Regions

Recent market analysis reveals accelerating rental growth in five English regions, with experts linking this trend to regulatory changes in the private rented sector. The increases come amidst ongoing housing supply challenges and evolving landlord-tenant dynamics following recent legislative reforms.

Regional Variations in Rental Market Performance

Data indicates particularly strong growth in certain areas, with the East Midlands and North West England showing some of the most significant price movements. Property professionals suggest several factors may be contributing to these regional disparities:

  • Variations in local housing demand and employment opportunities
  • Differences in rental property supply across regions
  • The impact of recent regulatory changes on landlord behaviour
  • Movement patterns of tenants leaving high-cost urban centres

Industry observers note that these regional price increases occur against a backdrop of generally tight rental markets nationwide, with tenant demand continuing to outpace available properties in many locations.

Understanding the Regulatory Context

The rental market shifts follow recent changes to tenancy regulations designed to improve standards in the private rented sector. While these reforms aim to benefit tenants through enhanced protections, some analysts suggest they may have contributed to current market conditions:

  • Some landlords may be adjusting pricing to account for increased compliance costs
  • Changes may have accelerated portfolio restructuring among property investors
  • The reforms coincide with broader economic pressures affecting the sector

Prospective renters facing these market conditions might consider reviewing their budgets and researching local rental trends when planning moves. Those considering longer-term tenancies may wish to explore options for securing current rental rates before potential further increases.

Market watchers will be monitoring whether these regional growth patterns persist in coming quarters and whether similar trends emerge in other parts of the country.

item.title: Rental arrears hit all-time low
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The proportion of tenants struggling with rental payments has fallen to the lowest level on record, according to recent industry data. Whilst this positive trend suggests improved tenant affordability, analysis reveals that landlords with larger property portfolios continue to face higher exposure to payment issues.

Rental arrears at historic lows

Market indicators show that tenant arrears have reached unprecedented lows across the UK private rental sector. This decline in late payments comes as welcome news for landlords, with financial pressures on renters appearing to ease following several challenging years. Experts suggest multiple factors may be contributing to this improvement, including stabilising living costs and stronger wage growth in some sectors.

Industry analysts note that the current arrears rate represents a significant improvement compared to pandemic-era figures. Whilst the exact figures vary between regions, the national picture demonstrates a clear downward trajectory in payment issues. However, specialists caution that this positive trend could shift if economic conditions deteriorate.

Portfolio size impacts risk exposure

Despite the overall improvement, data reveals an important distinction between different types of landlords. Those managing larger property portfolios reportedly experience notably higher instances of missed payments compared to landlords with just one or two rental properties. This discrepancy suggests that portfolio size remains a key factor in rental income reliability.

Several potential explanations exist for this pattern. Larger landlords often operate in different market segments, sometimes accommodating higher-risk tenants who may face greater financial instability. Additionally, the administrative challenges of managing multiple properties could contribute to delays in identifying and addressing payment issues promptly.

Considerations for property investors

For landlords and property investors, these findings highlight several important considerations. Those with multiple properties might wish to review their tenant selection criteria and payment monitoring systems. Implementing robust rent collection processes could help mitigate the additional risks associated with larger portfolios.

Furthermore, experts recommend maintaining contingency funds equivalent to several months' rent. This precaution could provide valuable protection against potential payment disruptions, particularly for landlords reliant on rental income. As market conditions continue to evolve, staying informed about regional trends in tenant affordability may also prove beneficial.

The current low arrears environment presents an encouraging picture for the rental sector. However, the variation between portfolio sizes serves as a reminder that careful portfolio management remains essential for all property investors, regardless of market conditions.

item.title: Residential construction starts down 15% on quarter
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK housing market has faced a notable slowdown in residential construction starts, with figures dropping by 15% in the last quarter. This decline has been attributed to several challenges facing developers, including sluggish sales, rising construction costs, and the impact of the building safety levy. Such factors have created a challenging environment for the industry, potentially affecting housing supply and affordability in the near future.

Challenges Facing Developers

Developers are grappling with a combination of economic pressures that have contributed to the slowdown in construction starts. Rising material and labour costs have squeezed profit margins, making it harder for firms to justify new projects. Additionally, the introduction of the building safety levy, designed to fund fire safety improvements following the Grenfell Tower tragedy, has added further financial strain. These factors, coupled with weaker buyer demand due to economic uncertainty, have led to a cautious approach in launching new developments.

Impact on Housing Supply

The reduction in construction starts could have significant implications for the UK’s housing supply. With fewer new homes being built, there may be increased competition for existing properties, potentially driving up prices. This could exacerbate affordability issues, particularly for first-time buyers already facing high mortgage rates and deposit requirements. Policymakers and industry stakeholders may need to consider measures to incentivise construction and address these supply challenges.

Whilst the current trends present obstacles for the housing market, they also highlight the importance of long-term strategies to support sustainable growth in the sector. Borrowers and investors might consider staying informed about market developments to make well-informed decisions in this evolving landscape.

item.title: Balearic investors switch to branded residences
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
Balearic Property Investors Shift Focus to Branded Residences

By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

UK investors in Balearic property are increasingly turning their attention to branded residences, as stricter regulations on holiday lets reshape the market. With popular destinations like Mallorca, Ibiza and Menorca introducing tighter rules on short-term rentals, many British buyers are exploring alternative options to secure returns from their overseas investments.

Why Branded Residences Are Gaining Popularity

The appeal of branded residences – luxury properties managed by prestigious hotel chains or developers – lies in their potential to offer more stable returns than traditional holiday lets. item.title: EYE NEWS UPDATE: All landlords ordered to register properties under new national scheme
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords across England will need to register all rental properties under a forthcoming national scheme set to launch in December 2026, according to a government announcement. The mandatory registration system aims to improve oversight of the private rental sector, with phased regional implementation planned over the following year.

New registration requirements for landlords

The "Register your rental property" initiative will first roll out in the West Midlands before expanding nationwide. Landlords will have a three-month window to comply once their local area joins the scheme, with full implementation expected by November 2027. The annual registration fee has been set at £65 per property, renewable each year.

Initially targeting currently let properties and those becoming occupied during the rollout, the scheme will later extend to vacant rentals. Future legislation will require landlords to register empty properties before marketing them to tenants. Both landlords and letting agents must display registration numbers on all property advertisements.

Financial penalties await those who fail to register, with local councils gaining access to the database to identify non-compliant landlords. The government also plans to give tenants access to verify their landlord's registration status before committing to a tenancy.

Part of wider rental reforms

This registration service forms the foundation for a comprehensive national database of private rented properties. Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook described it as "an important first step" towards implementing the government's Renters' Rights Act, designed to empower tenants while supporting responsible landlords.

In related changes, the government has announced reforms to rent increase challenges. Responsibility for initial decisions will transfer from the First-tier Tribunal to HMRC's Valuation Office, potentially streamlining the process for tenants contesting rental hikes.

The combined measures represent significant changes to England's rental landscape, with implications for landlords, letting agents and tenants alike. Property investors may wish to review their portfolio management processes in preparation for these upcoming requirements.

item.title: Low-deposit mortgage lending hits 18-year high
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The proportion of low-deposit mortgages has reached its highest level in nearly two decades, as more homebuyers turn to higher loan-to-value (LTV) products to get onto the property ladder. According to the latest Bank of England data, 8.4% of gross mortgage advances in Q2 2026 were at 90% LTV or higher – marking the highest share since 2008.

Why low-deposit mortgages are gaining popularity

With house prices remaining elevated in many parts of the UK, prospective buyers are increasingly relying on mortgages requiring smaller deposits. The current 8.4% figure represents a notable increase from 7% during the same period last year, highlighting how vital these products have become for first-time buyers and those struggling to save substantial deposits.

Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, noted: "Saving for a large house deposit remains a significant challenge, particularly amidst the current cost-of-living pressures. Lenders have responded by offering more competitive products at higher LTV tiers, though borrowers should carefully consider their long-term affordability."

Those considering high LTV mortgages may wish to be mindful of potential risks such as negative equity should property values decline. Seeking independent financial advice and considering overpayments when possible could help mitigate these concerns.

Mortgage costs remain elevated

The Bank of England data also reveals ongoing pressure from higher borrowing costs. The proportion of mortgages priced 2-3 percentage points above the Base Rate rose to 3.1% in Q2 2026 – the highest level since early 2023.

Springall added: "With economists suggesting the Bank Rate could rise further rather than fall in the coming months, borrowers might not see relief from high mortgage rates anytime soon. It's worth remembering that fixed-rate mortgages follow swap rates rather than the Base Rate directly, adding another layer of complexity to rate predictions."

Homeowners approaching the end of their fixed-term deals may wish to explore their options well in advance, as shopping around could help secure more favourable terms.

Arrears show modest improvement

In more positive news, mortgage arrears have shown a slight improvement. The value of outstanding balances in arrears fell by 1.9% during the quarter to £19.7bn – the lowest figure since Q3 2023. The proportion of total mortgage balances in arrears remained steady at 1.1%.

This suggests that while higher interest rates continue to put pressure on household budgets, most borrowers are managing to keep up with repayments. However, experts caution that financial challenges persist for some households, particularly those on variable rate mortgages.

As the mortgage landscape evolves, staying informed about market trends and seeking professional advice could help borrowers make decisions suited to their individual circumstances.

item.title: Letting agents call for greater clarity over rent tribunals
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

As the rental sector adapts to the Renters’ Rights Act, industry experts are calling for improved clarity around rent tribunal processes. Propertymark, the professional body for property agents, highlights the need for simpler guidance and better support for both landlords and tenants navigating the First-tier Tribunal system.

Demands for clearer tribunal processes

The newly implemented rules require landlords in England to follow the Section 13 procedure when increasing rents for periodic tenancies, providing tenants with at least two months' notice. However, concerns have been raised about the complexity of challenging these increases through the tribunal system.

Greg Tsuman, former ARLA Propertymark president, emphasised the importance of accessible information: "We need much clearer guidance, simplified forms and practical advice for tenants considering challenging rent rises before they take effect." He also noted the tribunal's focus on actual achieved rents rather than advertised prices – a crucial distinction that both parties should understand.

Additional improvements suggested include enhancing the tribunal helpline service with properly trained staff capable of offering accurate legal guidance. These changes could help prevent unnecessary tribunal cases by ensuring both landlords and tenants better comprehend their rights and obligations.

The value of early intervention

Propertymark is encouraging letting agents to initiate affordability discussions with tenants before landlords serve Section 13 notices. Current president Kim Lidbury explained how proactive conversations could resolve issues before they escalate: "Tenants sometimes use rent increase notices to raise unrelated concerns, or may not disclose their full circumstances. Early dialogue could prevent unnecessary tribunal applications."

Maintaining tenancies benefits all parties, Lidbury added: "Most landlords have ongoing costs and responsibilities, while tenants benefit from stability. Prolonged occupancy generally represents the best outcome for both sides."

Tsuman reinforced that negotiation often presents a preferable alternative to formal proceedings: "Legislation doesn't prevent landlords and tenants from reaching mutual agreements outside the tribunal system. In many cases, constructive discussions can avoid the time and expense of legal processes."

The agent's role in dispute resolution

Letting agents can play a pivotal part in facilitating these discussions, helping landlords set reasonable rent increases while ensuring tenants' concerns are properly addressed. Propertymark suggests this mediation could reduce tribunal cases while maintaining fair outcomes for both parties.

As the rental market continues to adapt to legislative changes, clearer processes and improved communication channels may help create a more efficient system for handling rent disputes – ultimately benefiting landlords, tenants and letting professionals alike.

item.title: Renters squeezed as asking rents outstrip budgets
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New research highlights the growing financial strain on UK renters, with nearly 40% now spending over half their income on rent alone. Data from flatshare platform SpareRoom reveals a widening gap between what tenants can afford and what landlords are asking, forcing many to make difficult housing decisions.

Rent costs outpace tenant budgets

SpareRoom's analysis of Q2 2026 data shows average room rents exceeded tenants' budgets in half of the 35 major cities surveyed. The situation appears most severe in Edinburgh, where the average £834 monthly room rent sits £86 above typical renter budgets - an annual shortfall exceeding £1,000. York and Derby follow closely, with yearly affordability gaps of £611 and £607 respectively.

The research identified several other cities where rental prices consistently outstrip what flatsharers can pay:

  • Belfast (£38 monthly gap)
  • Glasgow (£36 monthly gap)
  • Cardiff (£35 monthly gap)
  • Birmingham (£29 monthly gap)

Financial pressure forcing moves

The affordability crisis is having real-world consequences, with SpareRoom's July 2026 survey revealing 32% of UK renters had been compelled to relocate in the past year due to unaffordable rents. Traditional budgeting advice suggesting housing costs shouldn't exceed 30% of income now seems unrealistic for many, with just 15.3% of renters achieving this benchmark.

By contrast, 37.8% of respondents reported spending over half their income on rent (excluding bills) - a situation that leaves little room for other essential expenses or savings. This financial squeeze may explain why increasing numbers of renters are considering alternative options, including moving to cheaper areas or exploring shared accommodation.

For those struggling with rental costs, it could be worth reviewing all available housing options. Some renters might consider negotiating longer tenancies in exchange for fixed rental rates, while others may wish to explore whether they could potentially transition to homeownership with current government support schemes.

item.title: Lettings portfolios become hot property in estate agency acquisition race
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK estate agency sector is undergoing a significant transformation, with lettings portfolios becoming a prime focus for acquisition activity. According to research by The Business Acquisitions Group (BAG), buyers are increasingly prioritising recurring managed lettings income over acquiring entire agencies. This trend reflects a broader shift in the market, driven by private equity-backed businesses and evolving buyer strategies.

Why Lettings Portfolios Are in Demand

Managed lettings portfolios offer a steady stream of income, making them an attractive proposition for buyers. Unlike sales income, which can fluctuate with market conditions, lettings provide consistent revenue. This stability is particularly appealing in uncertain economic times. Recent examples include Lomond’s acquisition of Edward Mellor’s lettings division and Dwelly’s purchase of AP Morgan’s lettings business, both highlighting this growing trend.

Martin Bunney, founder and managing director of BAG, notes that buyers are increasingly assessing the sales and lettings elements of agencies separately. “Sales income is welcome, but all serious buyers are now competing for managed income,” he explains. For sellers, ensuring their lettings portfolio is well-maintained and organised could enhance its appeal to potential buyers.

The Role of Private Equity in Consolidation

Private equity-backed platforms are playing an increasingly prominent role in the acquisition market. These platforms are often well-funded and strategically focused on building substantial lettings portfolios. Campions Group, the UK arm of French group Emeria, is one such active buyer, particularly in London.

New sources of acquisition finance are also broadening the pool of potential purchasers. For example, property investment business Sourced launched a programme in 2025 offering franchisees funding to acquire letting agencies. This development has further intensified competition in the market.

Implications for Estate Agency Owners

For owners of combined sales and lettings agencies, this shift in buyer focus could influence their exit strategies. Bunney observes that the acquisition market has evolved, with buyer strategy moving away from entire agencies by large franchise groups to lettings books by private equity platforms. This change may prompt agency owners to consider separating their sales and lettings businesses to maximise their value.

The research by BAG underscores the importance of understanding these market dynamics. With lettings portfolios now a hot commodity, agency owners might wish to evaluate their options carefully, particularly if they are considering selling. Ensuring their lettings business is in good shape could make it a more attractive proposition in this competitive landscape.

As the estate agency sector continues to consolidate, lettings portfolios are likely to remain a key focus for buyers. With private equity-backed platforms driving much of this activity, the market is set to evolve further in the coming years.

item.title: Estate agents not to blame for property sale delays – Rightmove
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

When it comes to property transactions, delays can be frustrating for all parties involved. However, recent research from Rightmove suggests that estate agents are often unfairly blamed for these hold-ups. In reality, the majority of delays stem from other stages of the process, many of which are beyond an estate agent’s control. Understanding these factors could help homeowners better navigate the complexities of buying and selling property.

Where Do Delays Occur?

According to Rightmove’s findings, conveyancing is the most common source of delays, cited by 37% of home movers. This legal process, which involves transferring property ownership, can be time-consuming and often depends on external parties such as solicitors. Additionally, 15% of respondents highlighted survey or valuation issues as a cause of delays, while 11% pointed to problems with property searches. A further 11% experienced setbacks when another party withdrew from the transaction and needed to be replaced, and 9% attributed delays to chain-related complications. By comparison, only 5% of respondents identified poor buyer qualification as a factor.

The Role of Estate Agents

The research underscores the importance of recognising the role estate agents play in facilitating property transactions. While their work is often behind the scenes, they play a vital part in coordinating various stages of the process. Christian Balshen, director of agency partnerships at Rightmove, emphasised that many delays occur outside of agents’ direct control. He noted, “The work estate agents do is often underestimated because much of what they deliver happens behind the scenes. We want to help the public better understand the value agents provide.”

Rightmove is actively working to improve consumer understanding of the property transaction process. item.title: Estate agents pull ‘unsellable’ leasehold properties from market
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Leasehold properties are increasingly becoming a challenge to sell, with new research revealing that over three-quarters of estate agents have withdrawn such homes from the market due to their unsellable nature. According to Propertymark, 78% of agents have taken this step, whilst less than 1% reported that selling leasehold properties has become easier in the last two years. The trade body is urging the government to expedite leasehold reforms to better protect existing homeowners as the market transitions towards commonhold.

The Growing Challenges of Leasehold Properties

The research, based on responses from over 1,200 leaseholders and 200 Propertymark members, paints a concerning picture. A staggering 93% of leaseholders stated they would not purchase a leasehold property again, citing issues such as escalating service charges and difficulties in challenging unfair fees. Service charges, in particular, have emerged as a significant barrier to sales, with 74% of agents identifying them as a major obstacle. Some reported cases where annual charges doubled from £1,000-£2,000 to £3,000-£4,000, raising affordability concerns for potential buyers and even affecting mortgage eligibility.

Delays in obtaining necessary information for leasehold transactions further complicate the process. Around 40% of agents noted that securing the required details can take more than 15 days, sometimes stretching to several months. Only 17% typically receive the information within five days. These delays can frustrate buyers and sellers alike, adding to the already complex nature of leasehold transactions.

Building Safety Concerns and the Need for Reform

Building safety defects continue to cast a shadow over leasehold properties, further hindering sales. Propertymark’s analysis highlights the ongoing impact of these issues, particularly in England, where remediation efforts for affected flats are still underway. The combination of rising service charges, building safety concerns, and bureaucratic delays has left many leaseholders in a difficult position, with some finding their properties effectively unsellable.

Timothy Douglas, Head of Policy and Campaigns at Propertymark, emphasised the urgency of reform. He noted that whilst the move towards commonhold is welcome, existing leaseholders cannot afford to wait decades for change. Immediate action is needed to address unaffordable service charges, building safety problems, and the broader challenges faced by homeowners. Douglas called on the UK government to act swiftly to restore confidence in the market and provide much-needed support to leaseholders and property professionals.

As the leasehold system faces mounting criticism, homeowners may wish to carefully consider their options when buying or selling leasehold properties. Whilst reforms are on the horizon, the current challenges highlight the importance of understanding the implications of leasehold ownership and staying informed about potential changes in legislation.

item.title: Letting agents face £40,000 penalties as licensing rules expand
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Letting agents and landlords across England could face penalties of up to £40,000 for licensing breaches as local authorities expand regulation in the private rented sector. With councils introducing new selective and additional licensing schemes, industry body Propertymark is urging property professionals to stay informed about local requirements.

Higher penalties now in force

The first phase of the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect on 1st May 2026, has increased the maximum civil penalty for Housing Act offences from £30,000 to £40,000. Councils can now impose these substantial fines for offences including operating a House in Multiple Occupation (HMO) without the required licence or breaching licence conditions. The changes form part of a broader trend towards stricter enforcement in the private rental market.

Growing complexity in licensing requirements

Local authorities across England are currently considering new or expanded licensing schemes, with some councils also exploring Article 4 Directions affecting HMOs. Propertymark highlights how these local regulations, combined with higher penalties, have created an increasingly complex compliance landscape for agents and landlords.

Operating an unlicensed property carries multiple risks beyond civil penalties. Those managing properties may face liability, and landlords in rent-to-rent arrangements could find themselves responsible for compliance failures. In some cases, councils and tenants may pursue rent repayment orders, potentially reclaiming up to two years' rent where proper licensing hasn't been obtained.

Industry calls for proportionate regulation

Tim Thomas of Propertymark commented: "The regulatory landscape for the private rented sector is becoming increasingly complex, with rising costs for compliance failures. It's essential that agents and landlords fully understand licensing requirements, applicable conditions and responsibilities within property ownership structures."

While acknowledging licensing's role in maintaining standards, Propertymark advocates for evidence-based schemes that avoid unnecessary bureaucracy. The organisation stresses that responsible landlords and professional agents should not be hindered by excessive administration or inconsistent local requirements that could limit housing supply.

Looking ahead, the planned Private Rented Sector Database, set for regional rollout from late 2026, will introduce another compliance layer. While supporting the principle of a national register, Propertymark emphasises the need for better coordination between different regulatory systems to avoid duplicating requirements for compliant operators.

For landlords and agents, staying informed about local licensing schemes and maintaining up-to-date records has become more crucial than ever. With financial penalties increasing and new regulations emerging, thorough due diligence could help property professionals navigate this evolving landscape.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property and mortgage sectors are witnessing notable shifts as industry professionals make strategic career moves. From high-profile departures to key appointments, these changes highlight evolving trends in the market, particularly the growing appeal of self-employed brokerage models and the strengthening of leadership teams in established agencies.

Senior Director Joins Moveli After Two Decades at Savills

David Johnston, a seasoned estate agent with over 23 years of experience, has left Savills after 21 years to join Moveli, a self-employed brokerage firm. Johnston, who previously served as a director in Savills’ country sales team in Sevenoaks, brings extensive knowledge of the local market to his new role. His departure marks a significant shift from the traditional agency model to the increasingly popular self-employed approach.

Moveli, which focuses on the upper end of the residential market, has seen rapid growth in recent years. According to TwentyEA data, self-employed agents now account for 2.5% of the UK residential market share, representing an 18.6% increase compared to 2025. The firm boasts a network of over 100 agents and continues to invest heavily in proprietary technology to enhance its offerings.

Ben Littlewood, co-founder of Moveli, commented on Johnston’s appointment, stating, “David is an exceptional agent, and his move to Moveli speaks volumes about the changing market dynamics and the strength of our brand. We anticipate further growth and success as we attract more high-calibre brokers and expand our presence in the upper market.”

Landstones Strengthens Leadership Team

In another significant development, South West London estate agency Landstones has appointed Mo Kanso as its managing director. Kanso brings a wealth of experience from the residential property sector, including a previous role at Draker Lettings, where he played a key role in expanding the firm’s lettings department and opening new offices.

At Landstones, Kanso will focus on enhancing the agency’s presence across its core markets, with particular emphasis on SW6. He noted, “SW6 is a crucial market for us, and Landstones has consistently performed well in this area. I look forward to driving further growth and strengthening our position in the region.”

Expertise Added to Norton Rose Fulbright

Meanwhile, global law firm Norton Rose Fulbright has bolstered its real estate team with the appointment of Simon Woodcock as a partner. Woodcock’s extensive expertise in property law is expected to further enhance the firm’s capabilities in handling complex real estate transactions and advising clients in the sector.

These appointments and career moves underscore the dynamic nature of the UK property and mortgage markets. As professionals adapt to evolving trends and new opportunities, their contributions are likely to shape the future of the industry.

For homeowners and property investors, staying informed about these developments could provide valuable insights into market trends and the expertise available to support their decisions.
